title: Salem Witchcraft Trials: More Bonkers Than You Know
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant examine the 1692 Salem witch trials in Massachusetts Bay Colony: why the panic happened, the Parris girls' accusations, Tituba, Sarah Good and Sarah Osborne, the jail conditions, the Mathers and William Stoughton, spectral evidence, the Court of Oyer and Terminer and the executions, Giles Corey's pressing death, George Corwin and Philip English, Governor Phips dissolving the court, and Samuel Sewell's apology. The episode closes with a listener mail about a listener's father and the show.

segments.title: Opening banter on Salem and The Crucible
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the spooky Salem topic, discuss why the trials are hard to understand, and mention movies such as The Witch and The Crucible.

segments.title: Small-town conditions and Puritan litigiousness
segments.summary: Historian John Demos's explanation of why accusations arise in small, stressed colonial towns is discussed, along with the land disputes and quarrelsome nature of Salem Village and Salem Town and Puritan litigiousness. Puritan intolerance and the range of views among Puritan leaders are also covered.

segments.title: Increase and Cotton Mather and the first accusations
segments.summary: The Mather father and son are introduced as believers in witchcraft and demons. The hosts describe Betty Parris and Abigail Williams falling ill, the doctor's diagnosis of bewitchment, and the open question of what caused the girls' symptoms.

segments.title: Tituba, first accused women, and the jails
segments.summary: The girls name Tituba, then Sarah Good and Sarah Osborne. The hosts discuss why these women were targets and how accusations spread. The jail conditions are described, including the arrest and long detention of four-year-old Dorothy Good and the death of an infant born in jail.

segments.title: Governor Phipps, the Court of Oyer and Terminer, and spectral evidence
segments.summary: The hosts describe the backlog of more than a hundred accused people, Governor William Phipps's return, King Philip's War context, the creation of the Court of Oyer and Terminer under Stoughton, and the acceptance of spectral evidence. Other evidence types and tests are covered, along with Cotton Mather's reported caution about spectral evidence.

segments.title: Executions, Giles Corey, and social order breakdown
segments.summary: Bridget Bishop is the first person hanged in June. The hosts discuss the speed of the proceedings, Giles Corey's testimony against his wife and his recanting, and how children accusing adults overturned the social order. Rebecca Nurse, an upstanding woman, is also executed.

segments.title: Final tally, pressing, George Corwin, and Philip English
segments.summary: The hosts cover the death toll and deaths in prison, including Lydia Dustin. Giles Corey's pressing death is described. George Corwin, the sheriff who seized property, dies, and Philip English seizes Corwin's body to force repayment.

segments.title: End of the trials and Samuel Sewell's apology
segments.summary: Governor Phipps dissolves the court and creates a new one without spectral evidence, leading to releases. The hosts reflect on the witch hunt term and McCarthyism, and note Samuel Sewell's later public apology. Recommended resources are mentioned.

segments.title: Listener mail from CJ about dad
segments.summary: A listener named CJ writes that the show helps them reconnect with their father, who the host Chuck resembles. The hosts read the email and respond.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank the listener and close the episode with the show's credits.
